items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic CPU consumption in constructed BIT STRING decoding
items.description:
## Summary

In pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during `decode()`; no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.

The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an `asn1Spec`. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a **definite-length** constructed BIT STRING when given a matching `asn1Spec` and reaches the same vulnerable code. Constructed BIT STRING is not valid DER; this DER exposure is due to decoder permissiveness. DER rejects the indefinite-length form.

This is a separate decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER accumulation fixed in [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj).

## Technical details

In the 0.6.4 [`BitStringPayloadDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L173-L301), both the [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L237-L255) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L275-L301) fragment loops call `BitString.fromOctetString(..., prepend=bitString)` for every fragment. [`fromOctetString`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/type/univ.py#L614-L627) shifts the growing `SizedInteger` left by the fragment's bit length and ORs in the fragment. Shifting an ever-larger Python integer for each fixed-size fragment makes total work O(n²) for n fragments. The fragments are siblings, so the decoder's nesting-depth limit does not constrain their count; its limit on the number of length octets does not prevent the demonstrated inputs.

In 0.6.4, DER's [tag-driven map](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L40) disables constructed BIT STRING, while its schema-driven type map retains the inherited decoder that permits it. This explains why a schema-less DER rejection is not a negative result for all DER decoding.

Under [X.690](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en), a conforming CER constructed BIT STRING uses an indefinite-length outer encoding and primitive fragments with 1000 contents octets except possibly the last. That form reaches the affected indefinite-length loop. DER requires primitive string encoding, although the schema-driven pyasn1 decoder accepts the definite-length constructed example below.

## Impact

An application is exposed when untrusted input can reach one of the affected decoder paths and its input limits admit enough fragments. The work occupies the decoding thread or worker and may cause denial of service. Whether the input is network-accessible or unauthenticated depends on the calling application. This advisory makes no claim that every application using pyasn1, or any particular protocol implementation, accepts such input.

## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)

The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER values trigger the issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted values could occupy a finite decoder-worker pool and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not claim that every application is network-exposed or fully unavailable; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).

## Reproducer

The definite-length example below is valid BER. It is deliberately not a conforming CER or DER encoding. The second constructor uses conforming CER fragment sizing and framing. CPU times are machine-dependent; run the larger cases only in a local test environment.

```python
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber_decoder
from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer_decoder
from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der_decoder
from pyasn1.error import PyAsn1Error
from pyasn1.type import univ


def encode_length(size):
    octets = size.to_bytes((size.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")
    return bytes((0x80 | len(octets),)) + octets


def definite_fragments(count):
    body = b"\x03\x02\x00\xa5" * count  # one data octet per BIT STRING fragment
    return b"\x23" + encode_length(len(body)) + body


def cer_fragments(count):
    # Each primitive fragment has 1000 contents octets: one unused-bits
    # octet (zero) followed by 999 data octets.
    fragment = b"\x03" + encode_length(1000) + b"\x00" + b"\xa5" * 999
    return b"\x23\x80" + fragment * count + b"\x00\x00"


def measure(label, decode, payload, **options):
    start = time.process_time()
    value, remainder = decode(payload, **options)
    print(label, len(payload), f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f}s CPU")
    assert not remainder and len(value) > 0


for count in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):
    measure(f"BER {count} fragments", ber_decoder.decode,
            definite_fragments(count))

for count in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000):
    measure(f"CER {count} fragments", cer_decoder.decode,
            cer_fragments(count))

sample = definite_fragments(1_000)
measure("DER with BIT STRING schema", der_decoder.decode, sample,
        asn1Spec=univ.BitString())
try:
    der_decoder.decode(sample)
except PyAsn1Error:
    print("DER without schema rejects the constructed value")
else:
    raise AssertionError("DER unexpectedly accepted schema-less input")
```

## Verification

Local measurements of the official v0.6.4 tag on CPython 3.14.8 used `time.process_time()`. A local 0.6.5 candidate containing the fix was timed on the same machine. Times are illustrative, not a guaranteed cost on other systems.

| Input | Size | v0.6.4 CPU | 0.6.5 candidate CPU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BER definite, 50,000 fragments | 0.20 MB | 0.530 s | 0.084 s |
| BER definite, 100,000 fragments | 0.40 MB | 1.915 s | 0.170 s |
| BER definite, 200,000 fragments | 0.80 MB | 7.392 s | 0.344 s |
| Conforming CER, 1,000 fragments | 1.004 MB | 0.163 s | 0.0035 s |
| Conforming CER, 2,000 fragments | 2.008 MB | 0.657 s | 0.0070 s |
| Conforming CER, 4,000 fragments | 4.016 MB | 2.582 s | 0.0144 s |

The definite BER input with 100,000 fragments also decoded through DER with `asn1Spec=univ.BitString()` in 1.949 s on v0.6.4, versus 0.172 s with the 0.6.5 candidate. Schema-less DER rejected the same input. Independent reports reproduced the old behavior on v0.6.4: one measured 21.1 s for a 1.28 MB definite-length value; another measured 7.25 s for a 0.8 MB value versus 2.8 ms for a primitive BIT STRING carrying the same data volume. These measurements were taken on different systems and should not be compared as a single benchmark series.

## Resolution

Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. The decoder assembles fragment bits in a `bytearray`, preserves decoded bit values including intermediate-fragment padding, and converts the complete payload to a BIT STRING once. This removes the repeated shift of the growing integer in both constructed decoding loops.

For applications that cannot upgrade immediately, enforce an application-appropriate limit on untrusted ASN.1 input size **before** passing it to pyasn1. Such a limit bounds exposure but does not change the quadratic behavior of 0.6.4. Where a protocol forbids constructed BIT STRING, rejecting that encoding before decoding also prevents this path.

items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic-complexity denial of service in binary REAL decoding
items.description:
## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.

This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.

## Root cause and affected components

For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:

```python
p = 0
while chunk:
    p <<= 8
    p |= chunk[0]
    chunk = chunk[1:]
```

Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.

The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.

## Impact

A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.

## Reproduction and evidence

The following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The `0x09` tag identifies REAL; `0x80 0x00` selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises `decode()` only.

```python
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber
from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer
from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der


def real_value(mantissa_octets):
    content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets
    length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")
    return b"\x09\x83" + length + content


for codec in (ber, cer, der):
    for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):
        substrate = real_value(size)
        started = time.process_time()
        value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)
        print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)
        assert not rest
        assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0)
```

The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit `aa05757`. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.

| Mantissa size | Reporter's BER CPU time |
| ---: | ---: |
| 50,000 octets | 0.328 s |
| 100,000 octets | 1.299 s |
| 200,000 octets | 6.043 s |
| 400,000 octets | 24.095 s |

The same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.

A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (`d43496f`, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls `float()`, `str()`, or `prettyPrint()`.

## Fix

pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one `int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big")` conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.

items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic-time denial of service in constructed string and indefinite-length ANY decoding
items.description:
## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.

The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length `ANY` is affected in BER and CER when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.Any`; DER rejects indefinite lengths.

This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj). It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or `ANY` loops.

## Technical details

In the [v0.6.4 BER decoder](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py), `OctetStringPayloadDecoder` appends each decoded fragment to a growing `bytes` value with `header += component` in both its [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L338-L351) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L368-L387) constructed forms. [`AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1403-L1430) similarly uses `chunk += component`. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For `N` fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with `1 + 2 + ... + N`, or O(N²).

The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.

The [DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L49) replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven `TYPE_MAP` retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus `der.decode(data)` rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while `der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString())` accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without `asn1Spec`. These inputs violate [X.690's DER string-encoding rule](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) and should not be described as valid DER encodings.

The original short-fragment, definite-length OCTET STRING reproducer is valid BER. The CER decoder accepts it, but it is not a conforming CER string encoding: X.690 requires an indefinite-length outer constructed string and 1,000 contents octets per fragment except possibly the last. A conforming CER-shaped constructed OCTET STRING with those fragment sizes also reaches the loop and shows quadratic growth. The indefinite-length `ANY` reproducer below can represent a CER `SEQUENCE OF OCTET STRING` and reaches the separate `ANY` loop when decoded with an `ANY` schema.

The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit and nesting-depth limit do not bound the number of sibling fragments in these examples. The BER reproducer below uses only a three-octet outer length field; all fragments have shallow nesting. There is no per-message fragment-count cap in v0.6.4.

## Impact

If an application passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 to the affected `decode()` or `StreamingDecoder` path without an adequate input or resource limit, a megabyte-scale value can occupy a decoding worker for seconds. Repeated inputs can exhaust available CPU. Whether this is reachable before authentication, or through a particular protocol, depends on the application; the library finding alone does not establish those conditions. No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.

## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)

The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER inputs trigger the string-reassembly issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted inputs could occupy all available decoder workers and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not assert that every adopter has such an endpoint or loses all service; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).

On the official v0.6.4 tag, local CPU-time measurements with CPython 3.14.8 on macOS arm64 gave the following results. Times vary by machine and Python runtime; the input-size scaling is the relevant observation. “Fixed” means the local 0.6.5 decoder fix applied to the same inputs.

| Decoder path and input | Fragments | v0.6.4 CPU | Fixed CPU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.40 MB | 100,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.340 s | 0.160 s |
| BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.80 MB | 200,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.886 s | 0.312 s |
| BER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.60 MB | 400,000 × 2 payload bytes | 2.738 s | 0.623 s |
| BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.30 MB | 100,000 × 1 payload byte | 0.459 s | 0.206 s |
| BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.60 MB | 200,000 × 1 payload byte | 1.245 s | 0.412 s |
| BER indefinite `ANY`, 1.20 MB | 400,000 × 1 payload byte | 3.980 s | 0.826 s |
| CER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.00 MB, conforming fragment layout | 1,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0089 s | 0.0022 s |
| CER constructed OCTET STRING, 2.01 MB, conforming fragment layout | 2,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0311 s | 0.0044 s |
| CER constructed OCTET STRING, 4.02 MB, conforming fragment layout | 4,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.1379 s | 0.0090 s |

For the same short-fragment layout, the original report measured up to 16.05 seconds for a 3.2 MB BER constructed OCTET STRING. An independent report on CPython 3.11.16/Linux measured 5.76 seconds for a 2.4 MB constructed OCTET STRING, versus about 0.005 seconds for a primitive OCTET STRING of comparable size. These are reporter measurements on different systems, not fixed performance guarantees.

## Reproduction

This example uses public decoder APIs. Run it with pyasn1 0.6.4 and increase `n` to observe the scaling. The final two calls show the DER paths accepted by v0.6.4; their constructed encodings are not valid DER.

```python
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber
from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer
from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der
from pyasn1.type import univ


def tlv(identifier, contents):
    length = len(contents)
    if length < 128:
        return bytes((identifier, length)) + contents
    encoded = length.to_bytes((length.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")
    return bytes((identifier, 0x80 | len(encoded))) + encoded + contents


def measure(label, decode, substrate, asn1Spec=None):
    start = time.process_time()
    _, rest = decode(substrate, asn1Spec=asn1Spec)
    assert not rest
    print(f"{label}: {len(substrate)} input bytes, "
          f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f} CPU seconds")


n = 100_000
octet_fragments = b"\x04\x02AA" * n
utf8_fragments = b"\x0c\x02AA" * n

measure("BER constructed OCTET STRING", ber.decode,
        tlv(0x24, octet_fragments))
measure("BER indefinite ANY", ber.decode,
        b"\x30\x80" + b"\x04\x01A" * n + b"\x00\x00",
        univ.Any())

# CER uses indefinite length and 1,000-content-octet primitive fragments.
cer_fragment = tlv(0x04, b"A" * 1000)
measure("CER constructed OCTET STRING", cer.decode,
        b"\x24\x80" + cer_fragment * 1000 + b"\x00\x00")

# These constructed encodings are accepted by pyasn1 but are invalid DER.
measure("DER OCTET STRING with schema", der.decode,
        tlv(0x24, octet_fragments), univ.OctetString())
measure("DER UTF8String without schema", der.decode,
        tlv(0x2c, utf8_fragments))
```

## Patch

pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the growing `bytes` accumulator with a list of fragments and joins them once after decoding in all three affected loops. The OCTET STRING base-class change also covers the inheriting character-string decoders. This removes the repeated copying while preserving the assembled decoded value.

## Workaround

Until upgrading, enforce application-appropriate limits on the size of untrusted ASN.1 input *before* passing it to pyasn1, and limit the CPU resources available to decoding workers. Applications that require DER can also reject constructed string encodings before invoking the decoder. The appropriate byte limit depends on the protocol and expected valid values.

## Credits and references

Reported by [alimony](https://github.com/alimony). Independently reported by [manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi), whose report identified the schema-driven DER route, inherited character-string decoders, and additional performance evidence.

- [pyasn1 v0.6.4 affected decoder source](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py)
- [ITU-T X.690, CER and DER string-encoding rules](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en)
- [CVE-2026-59885, separate OID decoder issue](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj)

items.title: pyasn1 has quadratic CPU use in schemaless BER/CER/DER container decoding
items.description:
### Summary

When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.

### Details

ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.

### Proof of concept

Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:

```python
import sys
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder
from pyasn1.type import univ


def enc_tag(tag_id):
    groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]
    tag_id >>= 7
    while tag_id:
        groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)
        tag_id >>= 7
    return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))


def payload(tag_ids):
    body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'
                    for tag_id in tag_ids)
    length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')
    return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body


for count in (3200, 6400):
    cases = (
        ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus
                       for i in range(count)]),
        ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),
    )
    for name, tag_ids in cases:
        wire = payload(tag_ids)
        start = time.process_time()
        value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)
        cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start

        assert type(value) is univ.Sequence
        assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''
        for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):
            component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)
            assert component.asOctets() == b'A'
            assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id

        print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3))
```

### Impact

Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.
Out-of-bounds read in Windows Win32 Kernel Subsystem allows an authorized attacker to disclose information locally.
Exposure of sensitive system information to an unauthorized control sphere in Windows MIDI Service Module allows an authorized attacker to disclose information locally.
Out-of-bounds read in Windows Network File System allows an authorized attacker to disclose information locally.
Out-of-bounds read in Windows iSCSI allows an authorized attacker to disclose information locally.
Heap-based buffer overflow in Microsoft Windows Codecs Library allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.

items.title: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains
items.description:
## Summary

The public CCG lexicon parser `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring` parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`matchBrackets` consumes a bracket body one character at a time with `inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]`. The `rest = rest[1:]` tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). `augParseCategory` drives a `while rest != "":` operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (`rest = app[3]`) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. The parser carries a recursion-depth guard (`MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500`) that raises on deeply nested categories, but both quadratic loops run on flat input whose nesting depth stays at zero, so that guard never fires. No bound is applied to line length or category width before the text reaches these loops.

```text
Affected functions:
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.matchBrackets       (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:149-172; tail re-slice at line 168)
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.augParseCategory    (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:223-268; APP_RE tail re-copy at line 250)
Public entry point: nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:271), also re-exported as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring.
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the CCG lexicon string parsed by an application causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The vulnerable path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with attacker-chosen input size, a few-megabyte payload costs tens of seconds per core, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust worker threads. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only; it does not wrap these pure-Python slicing loops, so it provides no protection here.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, regex 2026.9.10, CPython. Run the parser on the shipped public API.
```

```python
import nltk.ccg.lexicon as L

# Vector A: flat bracket body -> matchBrackets tail re-slice is O(n^2)
n = 400000
lex_a = ":- S\nw => (" + "a" * n + ")\n"

# Vector B: long operator chain -> augParseCategory tail re-copy is O(n^2)
m = 32000
lex_b = ":- a\nw => " + "a" + "/a" * m + "\n"

import time
for name, s in (("A", lex_a), ("B", lex_b)):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        L.fromstring(s)
    except Exception:
        pass  # downstream parse error is irrelevant; the CPU is already burned
    print(name, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")
```

```text
Negative control (":- a\nw => (a/a)"):   ~0.00007 s
Vector A (matchBrackets, flat body):     n=50k 0.078s | 100k 0.260s | 200k 1.046s | 400k 2.083s   (~4x per doubling => O(n^2))
Vector B (augParseCategory, operators):  m=4k 0.078s | 8k 0.215s | 16k 0.485s | 32k 1.329s        (super-linear)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application calls the public `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str)` (also reachable as `nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring`) on lexicon text the attacker can influence.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the body width (a run of characters inside one bracket) and the operator-chain length; neither is capped by `fromstring`.
3. **Path:** `fromstring` splits input into lines and routes each category through `nextCategory`, which dispatches to `matchBrackets` (Vector A) or into the `augParseCategory` operator loop (Vector B).
4. **Guard:** The only relevant guard is the `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500` recursion-depth check. On flat input the recursion depth is zero, so `if _depth > max_depth` is never reached; the width loops run unbounded.
5. **Primitive:** The tail re-slice `rest = rest[1:]` and tail re-copy `rest = app[3]` execute a quadratic number of string copies.
6. **Result:** Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a few-megabyte lexicon costs tens of seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the parsing thread.

## Bypass Evidence

The one protection present on this path is the recursion-depth guard `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500` (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:22), checked at lexicon.py:153 and lexicon.py:228. It defends only against nesting depth and raises a bounded `ValueError` for deeply nested categories. The quadratic payloads here are flat: a single bracket body or a single operator run has nesting depth zero to one, so the depth check provably never fires while the width loops consume quadratic time. This was confirmed by running the shipped parser: the payloads complete without a `ValueError` or a regex `TimeoutError` while consuming quadratic CPU (Vector A shows a clean 4x cost per input doubling). A repository search finds no line-length or category-width cap anywhere on the `fromstring` path; the regex source-length limit bounds regex patterns, not lexicon text. The strongest disproof attempt (that CPython in-place string concatenation makes Vector A linear) fails because `rest = rest[1:]` is an unconditional copy of the remaining input that the concatenation fast path cannot elide, and the measured 4x-per-doubling ratio confirms the quadratic empirically.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The width-slicing loops ship in every release carrying the CCG lexicon parser and are present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior long predates the recent regular-expression and recursion-depth hardening.

## Suggested Fix

Scan the bracket body and the operator chain with an index cursor into the original string (or a `collections.deque`) instead of repeatedly re-slicing or re-copying the tail, so each character is handled in constant amortized time. As defense in depth, impose an explicit bound on lexicon line length and category width at the `fromstring` chokepoint and raise a bounded error when it is exceeded, mirroring the existing depth guard. No configuration-only mitigation fully removes the exposure for a service that must parse untrusted lexicons; until a fix ships, callers should cap the size of accepted lexicon input and parse it under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py: matchBrackets, nextCategory and augParseCategory thread a cursor instead of re-slicing the tail; the trailing capture group is dropped; MAX_PARSE_LEN=100000 caps the input).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_89p3_fcch_88ph.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (scaling 4.4x over a 4x input; an over-cap chain is rejected by MAX_PARSE_LEN). The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe: vector A (bracket body, 100k vs 400k) 15.8x and vector B (operator chain, 8k vs 32k) 11.3x over a 4x input, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

items.title: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization via list.pop(0)
items.description:
## Summary

`Tree.chomsky_normal_form()` binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with `list.pop(0)`, which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

In the default right-factor branch the transform executes `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` inside a loop over the N children of a node. `list.pop(0)` is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). The left-factor branch instead uses `nodeCopy.pop()` (removing the last element), which is O(1) and linear overall, so the two branches differ only by this front-versus-back removal. No cap is placed on the child count of a node, and the public `Tree.fromstring` parser accepts an arbitrarily wide bracketed tree.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/transforms.py; right-factor sink at line 168, O(1) left control at line 179)
Public entry points: nltk.tree.Tree.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/tree.py:455, default factor="right"); nltk.tree.Tree.fromstring (nltk/tree/tree.py:592).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the tree that an application normalizes to Chomsky Normal Form causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with the attacker-chosen child count, roughly 1.5 MB of treebank input costs about 14 seconds on one core and scales as N^2 above that. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not wrap this pure-Python list loop.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Drive the public transform on a wide flat tree.
```

```python
import time
from nltk.tree import Tree

for N in (80000, 160000, 320000):
    s = "(S " + "(A a)" * N + ")"
    t = Tree.fromstring(s)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    t.chomsky_normal_form()          # default factor="right"
    print("right", N, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3), "s")
```

```text
right (default):  N=80000 1.972s | N=160000 5.004s (2.54x) | N=320000 14.518s (2.90x)   -> super-linear
left  (control):  N=80000 1.399s | N=160000 2.731s (1.95x) | N=320000  5.379s (1.97x)   -> linear
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application parses an attacker-influenced treebank string with the public `Tree.fromstring` and normalizes it with `Tree.chomsky_normal_form()`.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the number of children of a node (a wide flat tree such as `(S (A a)(A a)...(A a))`); no child-count cap exists in `fromstring` or the transform.
3. **Path:** `Tree.chomsky_normal_form` delegates to `nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form` with the default `factor="right"`.
4. **Guard:** None. There is no width bound on the loop, and the regex match timeout does not wrap this pure-Python list operation.
5. **Primitive:** `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` performs an O(N) front shift on each of N iterations.
6. **Result:** O(N^2) single-core CPU exhaustion; roughly 1.5 MB of input costs about 14 seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the processing thread.

## Bypass Evidence

There is no guard to bypass on this path: neither `Tree.fromstring` nor `chomsky_normal_form` caps the child count, and the regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps only regex matching, not this list loop. The finding was confirmed by fresh timing that isolates the cause: the right-factor default and the left-factor branch build the identical bounded head strings and copy the node once, so the only differing term is `pop(0)` versus `pop()`. The measured right-versus-left divergence grows with N (right rises toward a 4x per-doubling ratio while left holds near 2x), which proves a quadratic component beyond the shared linear costs. A relevant corroboration is that the inverse transform `un_chomsky_normal_form` was already rewritten to a single linear pass to remove exactly this quadratic class (see the comment at nltk/tree/transforms.py:195-201), while the forward default path retained the `pop(0)` idiom. The strongest disproof attempt (that the head-string join dominates and is linear) fails because that join is bounded and present in both branches and therefore cannot explain the branch-dependent quadratic growth.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The right-factor `pop(0)` idiom ships in every release carrying this transform and is present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open.

## Suggested Fix

Rewrite the right-factor binarization to avoid removing from the front of a list: iterate the children with an index cursor or a `collections.deque` so each step is constant time, mirroring the linear rebuild already applied to `un_chomsky_normal_form`. As defense in depth, bound the child count accepted for normalization and raise a clear error past a configurable maximum. No configuration-only mitigation removes the exposure for a service that normalizes untrusted trees; until a fix ships, callers should cap accepted tree width and run the transform under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3909 "Fix quadratic DoS in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization (GHSA-r53h-rw34-8h97)", merged 2026-09-23, merge commit 2f53e20ce on develop.

Fix commits: 457ebe349 (linear front consume in chomsky_normal_form) and 677857dca (refuse a binarisation that would nest a tree beyond MAX_TREE_DEPTH). Follow-up #3917 (merge 9ba132e43, commit f0686dea6) walks Tree equality and conversion with an explicit stack so the deep-tree tests pass on Python 3.10 and 3.11.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_r53h_rw34_8h97.py; verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (chomsky_normal_form scales 5.1x over a 4x input).

items.title: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in ConllCorpusReader SRL instance builder via nested span rescan
items.description:
## Summary

`ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances()` builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`_get_srl_instances` iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner `break` that stops only when a span tagged `V` or `C-V` containing the predicate word is found. When the sole head span is placed in the last span column, no earlier column matches, so the `for ... else: continue` construct traverses every span of every earlier column before matching. Over P predicates each scanning up to P columns of R spans, the cost is O(P^2 * R). The block is read whole with no size cap, and the grid-consistency check enforces only uniform column count, not a bound on P, R, or total work.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:394-424; nested rescan at lines 405-419)
Public entry point: nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:158-169).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can supply a CoNLL corpus that an application loads and iterates with `srl_instances()` causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable through any corpus-ingestion surface (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost is super-linear in attacker-chosen predicate and column counts, a roughly 1 MB crafted corpus pins a core for tens of seconds and a few megabytes reaches minutes. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not cover this pure-Python nested loop over the parsed grid. Exploitation requires the application to use the SRL-specific API on untrusted CoNLL data with `words`, `pos`, `tree`, and `srl` columns; a deployment that never calls `srl_instances()` is unaffected.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Stage a crafted CoNLL corpus under an authorized data root and iterate srl_instances().
Corpus construction: one blank-line-delimited block with P predicate rows and P SRL span columns, the sole "V" head span in the last column.
```

```python
import time, os, tempfile
from nltk.corpus.reader.conll import ConllCorpusReader

def build_block(n):
    # n predicates, n SRL columns; the single V head placed in the last column
    # (columns: words pos tree srl...): emit n predicate rows and n SRL span
    # columns, with the single "V" head span placed in the final column.
    ...

for n in (40, 80, 160, 320):
    root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    open(os.path.join(root, "c.conll"), "w").write(build_block(n))
    r = ConllCorpusReader(root, ["c.conll"], ("words", "pos", "tree", "srl"))
    t = time.perf_counter()
    list(r.srl_instances())
    print(n, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")
```

```text
Negative control (single predicate): n=40 -> 1.88 ms ; n=320 -> 4.45 ms      (flat)
Attack (P=R=n):  n=40 -> 0.022s (10 KB) | n=80 -> 0.148s (39 KB) | n=160 -> 1.164s (156 KB) | n=320 -> 10.002s (619 KB)
```

The attack timing rises about 8x per doubling of n while the file grows only about 4x, confirming super-linear cost driven by attacker-chosen predicate and column count; the single-predicate control stays in the millisecond range.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application loads an attacker-supplied CoNLL corpus (columns include `srl`) and iterates it with the public `ConllCorpusReader(...).srl_instances()`.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the predicate count P, the span-column count, and the placement of the single head span; the block is read whole with no size cap.
3. **Path:** `srl_instances()` calls `_get_srl_instances`, which pairs each predicate against the span columns via a doubly-nested scan.
4. **Guard:** The inner `break` on the first matching `V` or `C-V` head is defeated by placing the sole head span in the last column, so every earlier column is scanned in full. The path-containment sandbox bounds where files load, not how much work a block costs.
5. **Primitive:** The nested rescan performs O(P^2 * R) span comparisons with no work cap or timeout.
6. **Result:** Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a roughly 1 MB corpus costs tens of seconds and scales super-linearly, blocking the processing thread.

## Bypass Evidence

The only short-circuit on this path is the inner `break` that fires when a predicate's `V` or `C-V` head span is found. It is defeated by construction: placing the sole head span in the last span column means no earlier column matches, so the `for ... else: continue` traverses every span of every earlier column for every predicate. This was confirmed in source (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:405-419) and reproduced end-to-end through the real public `srl_instances()` API, where the attack timing scales super-linearly while a single-predicate control stays flat. The path-containment sandbox is a file-location control and imposes no bound on parse cost, and the regular-expression timeout does not wrap this loop. The strongest disproof attempts (that Python `range` membership is O(1) so the loop is linear, and that the `break` fires early) both fail: the O(1) membership test is evaluated once per span, and the number of spans traversed is exactly what the last-column head placement maximizes.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The nested rescan ships in every release carrying this reader and is present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior predates the recent regular-expression hardening.

## Suggested Fix

Replace the per-predicate linear search over all span columns with a single pass that indexes head spans by word position (for example, build a map from word index to the owning span column once, then look up each predicate in constant time), reducing the total cost to about O(P * R). As defense in depth, bound the predicate and span counts accepted from a single block and process untrusted corpora under a CPU or time budget. No configuration-only mitigation removes the exposure for a service that must read untrusted CoNLL SRL data; until a fix ships, callers should cap accepted corpus size and isolate the parsing worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a "Patch seven algorithmic-DoS and path/exec GHSA classes across all affected modules" (ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances builds a one-pass wordnum to spanlist index instead of rescanning per predicate).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_v8f3_6phw_6mh9.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (srl_instances scaled 3.9x over 4x predicates). The same probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe: VULNERABLE (45.8x over 4x predicates).

items.title: Guard Core: Quadratic ReDoS in built-in detection pattern freezes the event loop with a single request
items.description:
### Summary

A polynomial (quadratic) regular-expression denial of service in guard-core's built-in penetration-detection patterns allows any unauthenticated remote client to freeze **every** endpoint of an application for seconds per request, using only the default configuration. The triggering request completes without any detection match — no ban counter increments, no rate-limit violation is recorded — so it can be repeated indefinitely. Since guard-core 3.5.0, only *custom* patterns are executed through the compiler's timeout-protected `create_safe_matcher()`; all built-in patterns run as a bare, inline `pattern.search(content)` directly on the asyncio event loop. guard-core ≤ 3.4.0 ran built-ins through the safe matcher (verified in the 3.4.0 wheel, `_check_regex_pattern`), so this is a **regression introduced in 3.5.0** — and it silently undoes the protection credited to GHSA-rrf6-pxg8-684g (CVE-2025-54365) and the unbounded-quantifier remediation of GHSA-j47q-rc62-w448 (CVE-2025-53539) for every stock pattern, despite the changelog advertising "Safe regex execution with configurable timeouts to prevent ReDoS attacks."

### Details

**1. The pattern** — `guard_core/handlers/suspatterns_handler.py:519` (master `08780f1`), the built-in template-injection detector:

```python
r"\{\{\s*[^\}]+(?:system|exec|popen|eval|require|include)\s*\}\}"
```

On an input of `{` repeated N times, every one of the N−1 positions starts a `\{\{` match attempt and `[^\}]+` scans to end-of-string and backtracks once per position → O(N²). Note the sibling pattern at `:524` (`\{\%\s*[^\%]+...`) is **not** vulnerable — its delimiter `%` is excluded from the character class, keeping scans bounded — which confirms the root cause is the unbounded, non-excluding `[^\}]+`.

**2. The unprotected execution path** — `guard_core/handlers/suspatterns_handler.py:910-926`:

```python
if compiler:
    if category == "custom":
        safe_matcher = compiler.create_safe_matcher(pattern)   # executor + timeout
        match = safe_matcher(content)
        ...
    else:
        match = pattern.search(content)                        # ← inline, NO timeout
```

In enhanced mode (the default whenever a `SecurityConfig` is present — `_supports_enhanced_config()` is a duck-type attribute check a stock config always passes), all built-in patterns execute inline **inside the async coroutine**, blocking the event loop for the full scan. In guard-core ≤ 3.4.0, `_check_regex_pattern()` routed *every* pattern through `self._compiler.create_safe_matcher(pattern.pattern)` (verified in the 3.4.0 wheel, `suspatterns_handler.py:565-567`) or, without a compiler, through `_check_pattern_with_timeout` (4-worker pool + per-pattern timeout). The `category == "custom"` exemption appeared in 3.5.0.

**3. Default reachability** — penetration detection is on by default (`enable_penetration_detection=True`), query parameters are scanned by default (`guard_core/utils.py:843-865`), and the default scan window `detection_max_content_length=10000` (`models.py:765-770`) admits the full 10,000-character payload. A run of `{` survives preprocessing untouched.

**Measured** (CPython 3.14, guard-core 3.12.0):

| input | detect() wall time | event-loop lag (measured in-process) |
|---|---|---|
| `{` × 2,500 | 0.15 s | — |
| `{` × 5,000 | 0.46 s | — |
| `{` × 10,000 | **1.85 s** | **2.57 s cumulative** across the three calls |

Clean 4× per doubling — quadratic, not exponential. Profiling all built-ins against the payload attributes 1.766 s of the 1.77 s total to this single pattern (one-line fix: bound the gap, e.g. `\{\{\s*[^\}\s]{0,64}(?:system|exec|popen|eval|require|include)\s*\}\}`).

**Amplification:** every scanned value pays the cost independently (`utils.py:843-890` per query param/header; `utils.py:936-977` per JSON string field). A single 256 KB JSON body (the default `detection_max_body_inspect_bytes`) containing ~25 string fields of `{`×10,000 measured **44.03 s of continuous event-loop blockage from one request**, returning normally with no detection hit.

**Why rate limiting doesn't help:** guard-core defaults are `rate_limit=10` per `rate_limit_window=60` s (`models.py:369-375`), and the `rate_limit` check runs before `suspicious_activity` in the default pipeline. 10 × 44 s = **440 s of loop blockage per 60 s window from a single IP** — single-source saturation, no distribution needed.

**Framework reach:** any adapter embedding guard-core on an asyncio loop — fastapi-guard, flaskapi-guard (async deployments), djapi-guard (ASGI) — shares the loop with the application, so the freeze takes down every endpoint of the host application, not just the guarded routes.

### PoC

**guard-core only — no framework adapter needed.** Requires `pip install guard-core`, then `python poc_guard_core_redos.py`. Exit code 0 = freeze reproduced.

```python
"""PoC: event-loop ReDoS in guard-core (>= 3.5.0, <= 3.12.0), default config.

The built-in template-injection pattern is quadratic on '{' x N, and since 3.5.0
built-in patterns execute inline (pattern.search) with NO timeout — only
`custom` patterns get the compiler's safe matcher. One detect() call with a
10,000-char value blocks the event loop ~1.8s; a 256KB JSON body with ~25 such
fields blocks it ~44s. Runs on the asyncio loop that any adapter
(fastapi-guard, flaskapi-guard, djapi-guard) shares with the app.

Run:  python poc_guard_core_redos.py
Exit code 0 = freeze reproduced (max loop lag > 1s).
"""

import asyncio
import time

from guard_core.handlers.suspatterns_handler import sus_patterns_handler
from guard_core.models import SecurityConfig

LOOP_LAGS: list[float] = []


async def _loop_lag_monitor() -> None:
    while True:
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        LOOP_LAGS.append(time.monotonic() - t0 - 0.05)


async def main() -> int:
    config = SecurityConfig(enable_redis=False)  # defaults = enhanced mode
    sus_patterns_handler.configure(config)

    monitor = asyncio.create_task(_loop_lag_monitor())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.3)  # baseline samples

    for n in (2_500, 5_000, 10_000):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        result = await sus_patterns_handler.detect(
            content="{" * n, ip_address="203.0.113.7", context="query_param:q"
        )
        print(f"'{{' x {n:5d}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.2f}s  is_threat={result['is_threat']}")

    # let the starved monitor task wake and record the lag it just endured
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    max_lag = max(LOOP_LAGS)
    print(f"\nmax event-loop lag during run: {max_lag:.2f}s")
    print("VERDICT:", "FROZEN" if max_lag > 1.0 else "not reproduced")

    monitor.cancel()
    return 0 if max_lag > 1.0 else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(asyncio.run(main()))
```

**Observed output** (Python 3.14, guard-core 3.12.0):

```
'{' x  2500: 0.16s  is_threat=False
'{' x  5000: 0.51s  is_threat=False
'{' x 10000: 1.91s  is_threat=False

max event-loop lag during run: 2.57s
VERDICT: FROZEN
```

An end-to-end proof through the fastapi-guard adapter (default config, real uvicorn server, in-process loop-lag monitor) measured **1.75 s of server-side event-loop lag from one GET request returning HTTP 200** — available on request.

### Impact

**Kind of vulnerability:** Regular Expression Denial of Service — CWE-1333 / CWE-400. Polynomial (quadratic) runtime, O(N²), not exponential backtracking.

**Who is impacted:** every application embedding guard-core ≥ 3.5.0 with its default configuration (penetration detection enabled) in a single-process asyncio deployment. One unauthenticated request freezes all endpoints for ~1.8 s; one padded POST body freezes them for tens of seconds; repeated requests at only 10/min saturate the worker indefinitely. Because the payload triggers no detection match, no ban counter increments and nothing is logged as suspicious — the attack is invisible in guard-core's own telemetry.

**Fix directions:** (1) bound the quantifier in the template pattern (its `{%` sibling at `:524` is already safe because `[^\%]+` excludes the delimiter — excluding the delimiter, or bounding the gap, closes it); (2) route built-in patterns through the same `create_safe_matcher()` timeout path as custom patterns, restoring the ≤ 3.4.0 behavior that the changelog advertises.



## Reporter validation request

The fix ships in guard-core 3.13.0, now on PyPI. If you reported this issue, please install 3.13.0 and confirm it is resolved. You can reply in this advisory's discussion thread or open a new issue with the result.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

inet: reject unhashed sockets during established lookups

TCP established ehash lookups are lockless. The socket caches involved
use SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU, so memory can be reused before an RCU reader
that retained its old address has finished.

After a tuple match, __inet_lookup_established() and
__inet6_lookup_established() acquire a reference and repeat the tuple
check. They do not check whether the new object is hashed. If the
address is reused for a socket with the same tuple, the lookup can
acquire a reference to the new object and return it while its nulls node
is unhashed.

A PoC that drives reuse with a SYN cookie request socket reproduced the
crash. The new request socket is unhashed and has a NULL rsk_listener.
A lookup that had loaded the address of the old request socket acquired
the reference published by tcp_get_cookie_sock() and returned the new
object. tcp_v4_rcv() then read sk_state through the NULL listener.

The resulting crash was:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000012
  #PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode
  #PF: error_code(0x0000) - not-present page
  ...
  Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP NOPTI
  CPU: 4 UID: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/4 Not tainted 7.3.0-00591-g0e135910deec #1 PREEMPT(lazy)
  ...
  RIP: 0010:tcp_v4_rcv+0x44e/0x1280
  ...
  R10: 0000000000000001 R11: 00000000024ca8c0 R12: 0000000000000000
  ...
  CR2: 0000000000000012 CR3: 0000000103d50004 CR4: 0000000000770ef0
  ...
  Call Trace:
   <IRQ>
   ? raw_local_deliver+0xae/0x240
   ip_protocol_deliver_rcu+0x2d/0x180
   ip_local_deliver_finish+0x84/0x100
   ip_sublist_rcv_finish+0x5f/0x70
   ip_sublist_rcv+0x12a/0x1d0
   ip_list_rcv+0xfd/0x130
   __netif_receive_skb_list_core+0x223/0x250
   netif_receive_skb_list_internal+0x1d2/0x2c0
   ? try_fill_recv+0x39/0x7b0
   napi_complete_done+0x74/0x170
   virtnet_poll+0x445/0x600
   __napi_poll+0x27/0x1e0
   net_rx_action+0x2fe/0x3b0
   handle_softirqs+0xc2/0x2c0
   __irq_exit_rcu+0x74/0xd0
   common_interrupt+0x7f/0x90
   </IRQ>
  ...
  Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception in interrupt

After taking a reference, check whether the nulls node is unhashed in
both IPv4 and IPv6 established lookups. If it is unhashed or the tuple
no longer matches, drop the reference and restart the lookup.

Lookups racing with the TIME_WAIT hashdance, or with a request being
replaced by its child, now restart and find the new socket instead of
returning the old one.

Request sockets that were never inserted into ehash can have a nonzero
refcount, and a stale lookup can hold a transient reference. Therefore,
when SYN cookie, Fast Open, and request migration paths fail after
setting a nonzero refcount, release the references held by those paths
with reqsk_put() instead of freeing the request directly.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: stop processing a read response after a receive error

cifs_read_iter_from_socket() may call cifs_reconnect() before returning an
error.  The reconnect path aborts pending mids and invokes their callbacks.
The callback can then release the cifs_io_subrequest containing rdata.

cifs_readv_receive() nevertheless continues after a negative return and may
dereference rdata in cifs_readv_discard().  KASAN reports the resulting
UAF:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in cifs_readv_receive
  Read of size 4 by task cifsd
  cifs_readv_receive (fs/smb/client/transport.c:1284)
  cifs_demultiplex_thread (fs/smb/client/connect.c:1355)
  kthread (kernel/kthread.c:436)
  ret_from_fork (arch/x86/kernel/process.c:158)

  Freed by task 148:
  netfs_put_subrequest (fs/netfs/objects.c:267)
  netfs_read_collection (fs/netfs/read_collect.c:460)
  netfs_wait_for_in_progress (fs/netfs/misc.c:462)

Return the socket error immediately, as this path did before the iterator
conversion.  This also avoids adding a negative length to total_read.
